passage.title: Measure Twice, Cut Once
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Bank
passage.text:
Fresh cedar shavings curled across the garage floor as Leo reached for the hand saw. He wanted to finish building a sturdy birdhouse before the bluebirds returned to the backyard oak tree. His uncle Mateo, a carpenter for twenty years, tapped his flat pencil against the steel tape measure. Mateo reminded his nephew that checking every mark twice was the real secret of clean woodwork. However, Leo was too eager to hear the buzz of the saw to check his ruler a second time.

Leo eyeballed the top plank, drew a quick line by hand, and sawed straight through the red cedar. He lifted the two roof pieces to set them above the front wall, but a wide gap yawned at the peak. Cold rain would pour right through that crack and soak any nest inside. On the long wooden bench, the slanted roof board cut by Leo in a rush was checked by Uncle Mateo with a brass square. The metal tool showed that Leo's pencil line had drifted half an inch off the corner.

Leo sighed and looked at the short scrap of wood, wishing he could glue the wood back together. Uncle Mateo did not scold him or take the tools away. Instead, he pulled a fresh cedar plank from the rack and handed Leo the sharp pencil again. He asked Leo to inspect the brass numbers on the ruler before making a single mark.

This time, Leo hooked the steel tape tight against the end of the board and marked six inches in two spots. Next, he laid the brass square across both dots to draw a crisp, straight line from edge to edge. Before picking up the saw, he measured the plank one more time to make sure his mark was precise. His arm moved in a slow, steady rhythm as the fine teeth sliced along the outside of the line.

When Leo set the new roof piece onto the walls, the two cedar edges met at the peak without a gap. Even a thin sheet of paper could not slide between the tight joints. Uncle Mateo smiled and handed him four brass screws to lock the roof in place. As they hung the finished box on the oak branch, Leo knew that two extra minutes with a ruler had saved an afternoon of waste.

tier2Words.definition: Strong, solid, and built to last through rough weather
tier2Words.rootHint: Related to standing firm without shaking
tier2Words.contextClue: Leo wanted a strong cedar birdhouse that would protect bluebirds in the oak tree.

tier2Words.definition: Very excited and impatient to start doing something
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin 'acer' meaning sharp or keen
tier2Words.contextClue: Leo was so excited to use the saw that he skipped checking his ruler a second time.

tier2Words.definition: To look at something closely and carefully
tier2Words.contextClue: Uncle Mateo asked Leo to look closely at the brass numbers on the ruler before marking.

tier2Words.definition: Exact, accurate, and free from careless errors
tier2Words.rootHint: From Latin 'praecisus' meaning cut off cleanly
tier2Words.contextClue: Leo measured a second time with the steel tape and brass square to make sure his line was exact.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"On the long wooden bench, the slanted roof board cut by Leo in a rush was checked by Uncle Mateo with a brass square."

Who performed the action of checking the slanted roof board in this sentence?

options.text: Leo, who cut the slanted roof board in a rush
options.childFeedback: Leo is the one who cut the board in a rush ('cut by Leo in a rush'), while Uncle Mateo is the one who checked it with the brass square.

options.text: Uncle Mateo, who tested the board with a brass square
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'was checked by Uncle Mateo with a brass square' shows that Uncle Mateo performed the action of checking the slanted roof board.

options.text: The long wooden bench inside the garage
options.childFeedback: The long wooden bench is simply the table where the board was resting; a wooden bench cannot check a board with a tool.

options.text: The bluebirds waiting in the backyard oak tree
options.childFeedback: The bluebirds had not even returned to the backyard oak tree yet (Paragraph 1), so they were not inside the garage.

questions.provingSentenceText: On the long wooden bench, the slanted roof board cut by Leo in a rush was checked by Uncle Mateo with a brass square.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'was checked by Uncle Mateo with a brass square' shows that Uncle Mateo performed the action of checking the slanted roof board.
questions.parentExplanation: The phrase 'cut by Leo in a rush' describes the roof board, while the main passive verb 'was checked by Uncle Mateo' shows that Uncle Mateo performed the checking.
questions.retryHint: Look at the words right after 'checked by' in the Paragraph 2 sentence to see who tested the board with the brass square.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"Before picking up the saw, he measured the plank one more time to make sure his mark was precise."

What does the word "precise" most nearly mean as used in this sentence?

options.text: Exact and accurate
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'precise' means exact and accurate, because Leo hooked the steel tape tight, marked two spots at six inches, used the brass square, and measured one more time before sawing.

options.text: Quick and careless
options.childFeedback: Quick and careless is how Leo drew his first crooked line in Paragraph 2; in Paragraph 4 he slows down to make sure his mark is exact.

options.text: Hidden under sawdust
options.childFeedback: Leo drew a 'crisp, straight line from edge to edge' so he could see it clearly as he sawed along the outside of the mark.

options.text: Impossible to cut with a hand saw
options.childFeedback: Right after checking that his mark was precise, Leo sliced cleanly along the line with his hand saw, so it was not impossible to cut.

questions.provingSentenceText: Before picking up the saw, he measured the plank one more time to make sure his mark was precise.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'precise' means exact and accurate, because Leo hooked the steel tape tight, marked two spots at six inches, used the brass square, and measured one more time before sawing.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 4, Leo measures six inches in two spots, uses a brass square, and checks his measurement a second time so his mark is 'precise' (exact and accurate).
questions.retryHint: Look at how carefully Leo measures with the steel tape and brass square in Paragraph 4 before picking up the saw.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 2, why would Leo's first roof board have been unsafe for a bluebird nest?

options.text: The cedar wood had sharp brass screws sticking into the middle of the box.
options.childFeedback: Uncle Mateo doesn't hand Leo the four brass screws until the very end of the story in Paragraph 5, after the new roof fits tightly.

options.text: The front wall of the birdhouse was too heavy to hang on the oak branch.
options.childFeedback: The birdhouse was not too heavy for the tree—in Paragraph 5, Leo and his uncle hang the finished cedar box on the oak branch.

options.text: A wide gap at the roof peak would let cold rain pour inside and soak the nest.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 explains that because Leo eyeballed his first cut, a wide gap yawned at the roof peak where cold rain would pour right through and soak any bird nest inside.

options.text: Bluebirds never build nests inside boxes made of red cedar wood.
options.childFeedback: Both planks were red cedar wood, and Leo builds the successful birdhouse out of a fresh cedar plank in Paragraphs 3 through 5.

questions.provingSentenceText: Cold rain would pour right through that crack and soak any nest inside.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 2 explains that because Leo eyeballed his first cut, a wide gap yawned at the roof peak where cold rain would pour right through and soak any bird nest inside.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 states that Leo's crooked cut left a wide gap at the peak, and 'Cold rain would pour right through that crack and soak any nest inside.'
questions.retryHint: Read the second and third sentences of Paragraph 2 to see what problem appeared when Leo set the two roof pieces above the front wall.

questions.prompt: How do Paragraphs 2 and 4 work together to show how Leo changes during the story?

options.text: Paragraph 2 shows Leo rushing without measuring, while Paragraph 4 shows him carefully double-checking his marks with the tape and square.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 2 and 4 show Leo's growth by contrasting his rushed, eyeballed cut in Paragraph 2 with his careful, double-checked measurements using the tape measure and brass square in Paragraph 4.

options.text: Paragraph 2 explains why cedar trees grow in the forest, while Paragraph 4 explains where to buy brass screws.
options.childFeedback: Neither paragraph talks about forest trees growing or buying screws at a store; both happen right at the garage workbench.

options.text: Paragraph 2 shows Uncle Mateo cutting the wood, while Paragraph 4 shows Leo watching from the backyard.
options.childFeedback: Leo cuts the wood himself in both Paragraph 2 and Paragraph 4 while Uncle Mateo guides him.

options.text: Both paragraphs show that hand saws always cut crooked lines through cedar planks.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, the very same hand saw slices a clean, straight edge that fits without a gap in Paragraph 5, proving the saw wasn't to blame.

questions.provingSentenceText: This time, Leo hooked the steel tape tight against the end of the board and marked six inches in two spots.
questions.childTip: Paragraphs 2 and 4 show Leo's growth by contrasting his rushed, eyeballed cut in Paragraph 2 with his careful, double-checked measurements using the tape measure and brass square in Paragraph 4.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraphs 2 and 4 form a clear contrast: in Paragraph 2, Leo eyeballs the board in a rush and cuts a crooked edge; in Paragraph 4, he applies his uncle's advice by measuring twice and using the brass square.
questions.retryHint: Compare how Leo marks and cuts the first plank in Paragraph 2 with the steps he takes on the second plank in Paragraph 4.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which statement best expresses the central lesson Leo learns in the passage?

options.text: Brass screws hold wood together much better than glue or nails.
options.childFeedback: Using brass screws in Paragraph 5 is just the final step of assembling the roof, not the big lesson Leo learned from his mistake.

options.text: Only someone who has worked for twenty years can build a birdhouse.
options.childFeedback: Leo is a kid who successfully builds the tight-fitting roof himself in Paragraphs 4 and 5 once he slows down and measures twice.

options.text: Taking a little extra time to prepare carefully prevents wasted effort later.
options.childFeedback: Across the story, Leo learns that taking two extra minutes to measure twice with a ruler and square prevents crooked cuts and wasted wood.

options.text: Sawing fast is the best way to keep cedar edges smooth and tight.
options.childFeedback: Sawing fast in a rush is what ruined Leo's first plank in Paragraph 2; in Paragraph 4, he moves his arm in a 'slow, steady rhythm.'

questions.provingSentenceText: As they hung the finished box on the oak branch, Leo knew that two extra minutes with a ruler had saved an afternoon of waste.
questions.childTip: Across the story, Leo learns that taking two extra minutes to measure twice with a ruler and square prevents crooked cuts and wasted wood.
questions.parentExplanation: The central theme of the story is captured in Paragraph 5: taking two extra minutes to measure carefully saves hours of wasted materials and frustration.
questions.retryHint: Read the last sentence of Paragraph 5 to see what Leo realizes about 'two extra minutes with a ruler.'
